cards.front: Which molecules cross a lipid bilayer by simple diffusion, with no protein?
cards.back: Gases such as O2 and CO2, and small nonpolar molecules. Water crosses too, though slowly.
cards.quote: Gases such as oxygen and carbon dioxide and small nonpolar molecules dissolve in that core and cross it by simple diffusion, needing no protein.
cards.section: The wall and the one rule

cards.front: Why do ions and larger polar molecules such as glucose cross a bare lipid bilayer almost not at all?
cards.back: Leaving water for the bilayer's oily core costs them too much energy, so ions and sugars cross the bilayer in useful amounts only through proteins.
cards.quote: Ions and larger polar molecules such as glucose cross almost not at all, because leaving water for oil costs them too much energy.
cards.section: The wall and the one rule

cards.front: State the direction rule for passive transport. What do channels and passive carriers decide, and what do they never decide?
cards.back: A solute flows on its own only downhill in its own electrochemical energy (concentration push plus voltage push). Channels and passive carriers decide which solute crosses and how fast, never which way.
cards.quote: Channels and passive carriers only open a path: they decide which solute crosses and how fast, never which way.
cards.section: The wall and the one rule

cards.front: How can a membrane protein move a solute uphill in its electrochemical energy?
cards.back: By coupling it to something running further downhill: ATP splitting (a pump), light or electron flow (some pumps), or another ion's gradient (a symporter or antiporter).
cards.why: The coupled total must still be downhill.
cards.quote: To move something uphill, a protein has to couple it to something else running further downhill: ATP splitting (a pump),
cards.section: The wall and the one rule

cards.front: Water crosses a membrane through aquaporins. What decides which way it flows?
cards.back: Water's own energy difference, set mainly by the solutes on each side (and by pressure, in walled cells). The aquaporin only opens the path.
cards.quote: aquaporins open the path, and water's own energy difference, set mainly by the solutes on each side (and by pressure, in walled cells), decides the direction.
cards.section: The wall and the one rule

cards.front: Membrane potential, Vm, is defined as {{c1::the inside minus the outside}}, so a negative Vm makes the inside downhill for cations and uphill for anions.
cards.quote: The voltage push: membrane potential, Vm, is the inside minus the outside, so a negative Vm makes the inside downhill for cations and uphill for anions.

cards.front: What is an ion's equilibrium potential, E_X?
cards.back: The one membrane voltage at which the ion's concentration push and voltage push cancel exactly, so its net passive flux is zero.
cards.quote: For each ion there is one voltage at which the two pushes cancel exactly.

cards.front: A K+-selective membrane sits exactly at E_K. Do K+ ions stop crossing?
cards.back: No. Ions still cross, but equal numbers cross each way, so net passive flux is zero.
cards.quote: At E_X the ion's net passive flux is zero. Ions still cross; equal numbers cross each way.

cards.front: Nernst equation: zF × E_X = RT × ln({{c1::[X]out / [X]in}}).
cards.back: Derived by setting the ion's ΔG_in to zero and solving for Vm.
cards.quote: zF × E_X = −RT × ln([X]in / [X]out) = RT × ln([X]out / [X]in), because flipping a ratio flips the sign of its ln.

cards.front: For a +1 ion at 37 °C, each tenfold concentration ratio shifts the equilibrium potential by about {{c1::61.5}} mV.
cards.back: The often-quoted 58 mV per tenfold holds near room temperature.
cards.quote: Many books quote 58 mV per tenfold change in concentration. That figure holds near room temperature. At 37 °C it is 61.5 mV.

cards.front: For one ion, the electrochemical energy change on entering the cell is ΔG_in = {{c1::zF × (Vm − E_X)}}.
cards.back: Vm − E_X is the driving force. Keep the sign of z.
cards.quote: Step 3, take out the common factor: ΔG_in = zF × (Vm − E_X).

cards.front: At 37 °C (RT = 2579 J/mol), a cell at −70 mV has Na+ 145 mM outside and 12 mM inside. Compute ΔG for Na+ entering, and say which way Na+ tends to move.
cards.back: Concentration push: 2579 × ln(12/145) = −6.4 kJ/mol. Voltage push: (+1) × 96 485 × (−0.070) = −6.75 kJ/mol. Total about −13.2 kJ/mol: both run inward, so Na+ is steeply downhill into the cell.
cards.quote: Total: about −13.2 kJ/mol. Both slopes run inward, so sodium is steeply downhill into the cell.

cards.front: A membrane permeable only to K+ at 37 °C (RT/F = 26.73 mV) has [K+]in = 140 mM and [K+]out = 5 mM. Calculate E_K.
cards.back: E_K = 26.73 mV × ln(5/140) = 26.73 × (−3.332) = −89.1 mV. (61.5 mV × log10(5/140) gives −89.0 mV, the difference being rounding.)

cards.front: A cell with E_K = −89.1 mV is voltage-clamped and its K+ channels are opened. Which way does net K+ flow at −70 mV, and at −100 mV?
cards.back: Out at −70 mV; in at −100 mV. At −70, Vm − E_K = +19.1 mV, so ΔG_in = +1.84 kJ/mol (entry uphill). At −100, Vm − E_K = −10.9 mV, so ΔG_in = −1.06 kJ/mol.
cards.why: Concentrations are unchanged; the larger voltage push (−9.65 vs −6.75 kJ/mol) outweighs the same +8.59 kJ/mol concentration push.
cards.quote: At −100 mV, in. Vm − E_K = −10.9 mV, so ΔG_in = −1.06 kJ/mol.

cards.front: A single K+ channel has a conductance of 20 pS and behaves ohmically; E_K = −89.1 mV. What is its current at Vm = −40 mV, and in which direction (outward positive)?
cards.back: i = γ × (Vm − E_K) = 20 pS × 49.1 mV = 0.98 pA, outward (positive).
cards.why: 0.98 pA divided by 1.602 × 10^−19 C per ion is about 6.1 × 10^6 ions per second through one pore.
cards.quote: At Vm = −40 mV its current is i = γ × (Vm − E_K) = 20 pS × 49.1 mV = 0.98 pA, outward

cards.front: For chloride (z = −1), Vm − E_Cl = +10 mV. Which way does net chloride flow, and why does this differ from a cation with the same gap?
cards.back: Inward. ΔG_in = (−1) × 96 485 × 0.010 = −965 J/mol, negative. Because z is negative, the same Vm − E_X gives ΔG_in the opposite sign from a cation, which would flow out.
cards.quote: Because z is negative for an anion, the same Vm − E_X gives ΔG_in the opposite sign.

cards.front: A cell at 37 °C has [Cl−] 120 mM outside and 12 mM inside and rests at −70 mV. Using 61.5 mV per tenfold, find E_Cl. If chloride channels open, which way does net Cl− move?
cards.back: E_Cl = (61.5 / −1) × log10(120/12) = −61.5 mV. Vm − E_Cl = −8.5 mV, so ΔG_in = (−1) × 96 485 × (−0.0085) ≈ +820 J/mol: positive, so net Cl− moves out of the cell.
cards.why: Here the inside is more negative than E_Cl, so the outward electrical push beats chloride's inward concentration push.
cards.quote: That is why E = 61.5 mV × log10(ratio) gives the same answer as the ln form.

cards.front: Does a typical cell rest at E_K? Why or why not?
cards.back: Usually not. A real membrane is permeable to several ions, so the resting potential lies between their equilibrium potentials, pulled toward each by its share of the conductance. Many cells rest less negative than E_K.
cards.quote: Many cells rest less negative than E_K for exactly this reason.

cards.front: How does a carrier's mechanism differ from a channel's?
cards.back: An open channel is an aqueous pore connecting both sides at once. A carrier binds its solute on one side, changes shape and releases it on the other; ideally its site is never open to both sides at once (alternating access).
cards.quote: A carrier binds its solute on one side, changes shape, and releases it on the other;

cards.front: Why does an open channel move ions so much faster than a carrier moves its solute?
cards.back: While open, a channel has no cycle to complete: millions of ions per second pass one pore. A carrier needs a shape change for every crossing.
cards.quote: while open it has no cycle to complete, so it is fast: millions of ions per second through one pore.

cards.front: Why does a carrier's transport rate level off as substrate concentration rises?
cards.back: It has a limited number of binding sites; once they are nearly always occupied, more substrate cannot speed it up. The curve follows Michaelis-Menten kinetics, like an enzyme.
cards.quote: because it has a limited number of binding sites, its rate saturates as solute rises, like an enzyme with Michaelis-Menten kinetics.

cards.front: What is a uniporter? Give an example.
cards.back: A carrier that moves one solute, such as GLUT1 moving glucose into red blood cells.
cards.quote: A uniporter is a carrier that moves one solute, as GLUT1 moves glucose into red blood cells.

cards.front: A red blood cell takes up glucose only through GLUT1. Glucose is 5 mM outside and 1 mM inside. What is the highest internal glucose GLUT1 can produce, and why?
cards.back: 5 mM, equal to outside. Glucose is uncharged, so only the concentration push counts; GLUT1 speeds it across until inside and outside are equal but can never concentrate it.
cards.quote: GLUT1 can speed glucose across, but with glucose alone, only until inside and outside are equal; it can never concentrate it.

cards.front: Per ATP split, what does the Na+/K+-ATPase of an animal cell move, and how much net charge crosses?
cards.back: Three Na+ out and two K+ in, so one net positive charge leaves per cycle.
cards.quote: The Na+/K+-ATPase in the plasma membrane of animal cells exports three Na+ and imports two K+ for each ATP it splits.
cards.section: Uphill by coupling: pumps, symporters and antiporters

cards.front: Distinguish primary from secondary active transport.
cards.back: Primary: a pump couples transport directly to an energy source, usually ATP hydrolysis. Secondary: a carrier spends one solute's gradient to move another uphill, with no ATP of its own.
cards.quote: Spending one solute's gradient to move another is secondary active transport.
cards.section: Uphill by coupling: pumps, symporters and antiporters

cards.front: Distinguish a symporter from an antiporter, with one example of each.
cards.back: A symporter moves two solutes the same way (SGLT1: Na+ and glucose in). An antiporter, or exchanger, moves them opposite ways (Na+/Ca2+ exchanger: Na+ in, Ca2+ out).
cards.quote: An antiporter (or exchanger) moves them opposite ways, as the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger brings sodium in and sends calcium out.
cards.section: Uphill by coupling: pumps, symporters and antiporters

cards.front: How does the Na+/K+-ATPase affect membrane voltage directly, and what is its main job?
cards.back: It moves one net charge out per cycle, making the inside more negative, usually by only a few millivolts (large in some cells). Mostly it builds the Na+ and K+ gradients other proteins spend.
cards.quote: In most cells that direct effect is small, a few millivolts, but in some it is large.
cards.section: Uphill by coupling: pumps, symporters and antiporters

cards.front: A drug blocks the Na+/K+-ATPase in intestinal cells. Predict uphill glucose uptake through SGLT1, at once and over time.
cards.back: It fails, but not at once. SGLT1 needs only that the coupled total, sodium's payment plus glucose's cost, is still downhill. As Na+ keeps leaking in, the payment shrinks, and SGLT1 can no longer pull glucose uphill.
cards.quote: With the pump blocked, the sodium gradient runs down as sodium keeps leaking in, the payment shrinks, and SGLT1 can no longer pull glucose uphill.
cards.section: Uphill by coupling: pumps, symporters and antiporters

cards.front: At 37 °C, each tenfold step uphill costs glucose 5.94 kJ/mol, and each Na+ entering releases 13.2 kJ/mol. What is the thermodynamic ceiling on glucose accumulation for SGLT1 carrying 2 Na+ per glucose?
cards.why: A ceiling, not a measured ratio: leaks and glucose exit keep real cells far below it.
cards.quote: That buys 26.4 / 5.94 = 4.44 tenfold steps: 10^4.44, about 27,500-fold.
cards.section: Uphill by coupling: pumps, symporters and antiporters

cards.front: A hypothetical Na+-glucose symporter carries 3 Na+ per glucose under the same conditions (13.2 kJ/mol per Na+, 5.94 kJ/mol per tenfold glucose step). Estimate its thermodynamic ceiling and compare it with the 2 Na+ case.
cards.back: 3 × 13.2 = 39.6 kJ/mol; 39.6 / 5.94 ≈ 6.67 tenfold steps, about 4.6 million-fold: roughly 166 times the 2 Na+ ceiling.
cards.why: Rests on the coupling rule: each extra Na+ adds the same payment, about 2.22 more tenfold steps (about 166-fold).
cards.quote: One extra sodium per trip multiplies the ceiling by about 166.
cards.section: Uphill by coupling: pumps, symporters and antiporters

cards.front: At −70 mV, exporting Na+ costs about +13.2 kJ/mol and importing K+ about +1.84 kJ/mol. Show that the Na+/K+-ATPase cycle obeys the downhill rule, given that ATP splitting in a cell releases roughly 50 to 60 kJ/mol.
cards.back: Cost: 3 × 13.2 + 2 × 1.84 ≈ +43 kJ/mol, less than the 50 to 60 kJ/mol from one ATP. Both moves are uphill, but the coupled total is downhill, with a margin.
cards.quote: Three Na+ out and two K+ in cost about 3 × 13.2 + 2 × 1.84 ≈ +43 kJ/mol.

cards.front: Why does a transport rate of millions of ions per second through one protein point to a channel rather than a carrier?
cards.back: Carriers typically cycle tens to a few thousand times a second, and even the fastest reach only tens of thousands. Millions per second needs a pore.
cards.quote: Carriers typically cycle from tens to a few thousand times a second, and even the fastest known reach only tens of thousands

cards.front: Which two numbers do you read from a one-channel patch-clamp record?
cards.back: The unitary current, i (step height, set by conductance and driving force), and the open probability, P_o (fraction of time open).
cards.quote: The unitary current, i, is the height of the step, set by the channel's conductance and the driving force.

cards.front: In a single-channel recording, what does a drug alter if it changes P_o but not i? And if it changes i?
cards.back: Changing P_o alone alters gating. Changing i alters conduction or driving force.
cards.quote: A drug that changes P_o without changing i alters gating; one that changes i alters conduction or driving force.

cards.front: A cell has 200 identical channels with a unitary current of 0.5 pA and P_o = 0.3. What is the mean current? Why can a whole-cell current alone not tell you N, i and P_o?
cards.back: I = N × i × P_o = 200 × 0.5 pA × 0.3 = 30 pA. Other combinations give the same total, such as 60 channels always open (P_o = 1) at 0.5 pA.
cards.quote: That is why a whole-cell current alone cannot separate N, i and P_o.

cards.front: A substance that cannot cross the membrane blocks a channel when added to the bath of an outside-out patch, but has no effect on an inside-out patch. Where does it act?
cards.back: On the extracellular face. In an outside-out patch the outer face meets the bath; in an inside-out patch the cytoplasmic face does.
cards.quote: In an inside-out patch, pulled off the cell, the cytoplasmic face meets the bath; in an outside-out patch, the outer face does.

cards.front: In a tracer-flux uptake experiment, which part of the time course gives the initial rate?
cards.back: The early, straight part.
cards.quote: The early, straight part of the time course gives the initial rate.

cards.front: Initial uptake rates (pmol/min) into matched vesicles: protein A gives 50, 83 and 91 at 2, 10 and 20 mM substrate; protein B gives 10, 50 and 100. Which behaves like a carrier? Estimate its Vmax and Km.
cards.back: A. It levels off toward a ceiling near 100 pmol/min (Vmax) and reaches half of it at 2 mM (Km), a Michaelis-Menten curve. B stays proportional to concentration, as a pore or simple diffusion does.
cards.quote: Look at the last two rows first: doubling substrate from 10 to 20 mM doubles B's rate but raises A's by about a tenth.

cards.front: Can channels saturate? How does the concentration range compare with carriers?
cards.back: Yes, but usually only at tens to hundreds of millimolar. Carriers often level off at micromolar to low millimolar substrate.
cards.quote: Channels can saturate too, but usually only at tens to hundreds of millimolar, while carriers often level off at micromolar to low millimolar substrate.

cards.front: Labelled substrate floods into carrier vesicles preloaded with unlabelled substrate, yet chemical assay shows the total substrate inside does not rise. What is the carrier doing, and why did the tracer suggest uptake?
cards.back: Exchanging: each trip brings one labelled molecule in and carries one unlabelled molecule out. A tracer counts traffic in one direction only; the outgoing traffic was unlabelled, so it went unseen.
cards.why: Label entering is not net uptake until you measure the total.
cards.quote: At first, label counts only inward traffic; the outgoing molecules were unlabelled, so the counter missed them.

cards.front: Given time, an exchanger can pile labelled substrate inside vesicles well above its 1 mM outside concentration. Why does this counterflow not break the downhill rule?
cards.back: Each labelled molecule that enters is paid for by an unlabelled one leaving down its own gradient, so the coupled exchange is still downhill overall.
cards.why: Rests on the coupling rule; this counterflow is a classic test for a carrier.
cards.quote: because each labelled molecule that enters is paid for by an unlabelled one leaving down its own gradient.

cards.front: Preloading vesicles with unlabelled substrate speeds labelled-substrate entry through a carrier. Does that alone prove the carrier is an obligate exchanger?
cards.back: No. A uniporter whose empty return step is slow also speeds up when preloaded. Faster label entry alone does not prove an obligate exchanger.
cards.quote: A uniporter whose empty return step is slow also speeds up when preloaded,

cards.front: CFTR, the chloride channel mutated in cystic fibrosis, belongs to the ABC family, most of whose members are ATP-driven transporters, and binds and splits ATP. Why is it still a channel?
cards.back: It uses ATP to open and close its gate, not to push chloride uphill; chloride flows through it downhill.
cards.why: Family does not decide mechanism; only functional tests do.
cards.quote: It still binds and splits ATP, but to open and close its gate, not to push chloride uphill: chloride flows through it downhill.

cards.front: Expressing an unknown protein Q in Xenopus oocytes raises their chloride permeability, but oocytes have their own chloride channels. How would you show that Q itself forms the chloride pathway?
cards.back: Compare with water-injected oocytes from the same frog and day. Then purify Q, put it into lipid vesicles and fuse them with a planar bilayer: chloride current with purified Q and no other protein shows Q is enough.
cards.why: High expression of many foreign membrane proteins switches on the oocyte's own chloride current.
cards.quote: If chloride current appears with purified Q and no other protein, Q is enough to form the pathway.

cards.front: You mutate a residue suspected to line Q's chloride pore. Mutation 1 changes the unitary conductance and which anions pass; mutation 2 changes only P_o. What does each tell you?
cards.back: Mutation 1: Q most likely forms the pore. Mutation 2 decides less: Q could be a regulator, or a channel whose gating you hit.
cards.why: Rests on the single-channel rule: i reflects conduction, P_o reflects gating.
cards.quote: If a mutation changes the unitary conductance or which anions pass, Q most likely forms the pore.
